claim: The test S2 is made to owe for 'an order with both a shortage and a bad percent asserts OutOfStock' pins an error precedence the owner never specified; dropping it leaves criteria 3 and 4 fully covered by the other owed tests and costs no owner-visible behaviour.

evidence.detail: The owner's text and criteria 3-4 define the shortage error and the bad-percent error separately; no line says which wins when both apply.

The stated reason for the owed tests ('a pass cannot be for the wrong reason — OutOfStock is itself a ValueError') is served by the `type(exc) is ValueError` assertions on the bad-percent cases; the combined-case test adds nothing to that purpose and only pins the ordering of D3.

D3's rejection of percent-first rests on 'it needs a second, duplicated range check in orders.py' — but percent-first is reachable with no duplication by calling pricing.apply_discount(subtotal, percent) before the stock pass (apply_discount validates the range itself, pricing.py:11-12). The ordering is therefore an arbitrary architect choice, not one forced by criterion 4.

The same section deliberately refuses to pin the repeated-sku case with a test so that 'the owner's answer must cost no test edit' — the combined-case test contradicts that stance for an equally unasked behaviour.

Some order between the two errors will exist in the built code; recording it in D3 as a decision is fine, but making it a test the slice must write turns an unasked ordering into a contract that a later owner answer (or a simpler one-pass implementation) would have to break.

traceability: none found — tasks/doing/010-order-quote.md criteria 3 and 4 each name one error; no criterion names a precedence between them
